newsitem.title: USA: Intel to encourage Web advertising in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Intel to encourage Web advertising in 1998.

text.p: Intel Corp, the world's largest maker of computer chips, said on Monday it will encourage personal computer makers to advertise on the World Wide Web next year in a programme which analysts estimate could raise annual Internet advertising by roughly $250 million.
The plan is part of the Intel Inside Program, which the company launched in 1991 to co-promote computer makers who use its Intel microprocessors in their products.

Intel said it has recently outlined its 1998 advertising plans for the programme in a letter to its 1,500 computer chip customers, and that 10 percent of the funds set aside for Intel Inside be spent on Web-based advertisements.

Intel sets aside six percent of each customer's chip sales to go towards the cost of advertising using the Intel Inside logo. The fund pays for 50 percent of the cost of television or Web advertisements, and two-thirds of the cost of print advertisements.
The programme has added up to large advertising spending -- more than $3.4 billion of advertising since its inception has contained the Intel Inside logo.
But 1998 will be the first year that Intel is delegating a percentage of the programme towards Web advertising, according to Kathy Melcher, a spokeswoman for Intel Inside.

Based on Intel's projected share of the $27.8 billion value that research firm Dataquest projects the microprocessor market to reach next year, as much as $1.25 billion could be set aside for Intel Inside.

Intel's 50 percent contribution to the Web advertising portion would amount to a figure of around $125 million, resulting in some $250 million in Intel Inside advertising spending next year according to projections, analysts said.

This compares with a survey by research group Cowles/Simba Information which found that Web advertising revenue in the first half of 1997 alone reached $217.3 million and was well on track to reach a projected $446 million for the full year.

Several Internet based media, including popular search engines and Web content sites whose business models are dependent on growth of advertising on their sites, said Intel's move would help boost the industry.
"It's the technology businesses that were the early provers of the value of online advertising," said James Desrosier, executive vice-president of marketing at Excite.
"I think the fact they're still sticking with it (Web advertising) and they're now saying we're going to put more clout behind it is an indication that it's working."
Intel would not comment on projected spending.

Melcher said Intel had experimented with Web-based advertising early, and now favours sponsored sites where it can show off applications of its technology over straight banner advertising on which visitors can click to read more.
